Commercial constraint: with payback at 34 months and 16 months of runway, the company is spending far ahead of when each customer becomes profitable, and implementation-delay churn shortens LTV before payback is even reached.

businessProblem: A Series B data platform growing 40% is acquiring and deploying customers at a cost its lifetime value can no longer support: fully-loaded CAC has risen to ~$220k, LTV/CAC fell from 3.4 to 1.6, and CAC payback stretched from 18 to 34 months, against only 16 months of runway. The cost stack is structural: a 6.5-month sales cycle with sales-engineering hours up 45%, plus a 16-week implementation the company subsidizes ~60% of (~$48k per customer), and ~40% of churned customers leave within 9 months over implementation delays, shortening realized LTV before payback is reached. The owner frames it as separate 'sales efficiency' and 'delivery' problems and weighs point fixes (more sales-engineering, more CS). But the binding issue is a unit-economics breakdown: the combined acquire-and-deploy cost exceeds supportable LTV, and at 34-month payback on 16-month runway the current motion is unsustainable. The owner must decide within a month how to restructure the economics, including segment focus, implementation pricing/productization, and deal selection.

evidence.finding: Fully-loaded CAC has risen to ~$220k (sales + marketing + sales-engineering + subsidized implementation), LTV/CAC fell from 3.4 to 1.6, and CAC payback extended from 18 to 34 months. At a 1.6 ratio and 34-month payback, the company spends far ahead of customer profitability, and the economics are below the threshold needed to be fundable.
evidence.source: Finance unit-economics model, CAC and LTV computation

evidence.finding: The sales motion is expensive and slow: average sales cycle 6.5 months and sales-engineering hours per deal up 45%, while win rate is stable at 22%. The rising SE intensity inflates CAC without improving conversion, indicating the cost of acquiring each customer is structurally high, especially in the largest deals.
evidence.source: CRM cycle data, sales-engineering time tracking

evidence.finding: Implementation averages 16 weeks and is heavily subsidized: the company absorbs ~60% of implementation cost, roughly $48k per customer, which is loaded into CAC. Implementation is genuinely complex (data migration, pipeline setup, governance), so the subsidy is a structural drag on acquisition economics rather than a one-off.

~40% of churned customers leave within the first 9 months, citing implementation delays and unrealized value, which shortens realized LTV before payback (34 months) is ever reached. Gross retention is 90%. Early-life churn does not just lose revenue; it directly worsens the LTV/CAC ratio by truncating lifetime on the most expensively acquired customers.

Segmentation matters: large enterprise deals have the longest cycles and most expensive delivery (and worst LTV/CAC) but highest ACV, while mid-size deals show materially better LTV/CAC. Competitors with simpler scopes run shorter cycles and cheaper delivery, pressuring the company's cost-to-acquire-and-serve in the enterprise segment.
